title: Fast Weight Attention: Which Pair Is the Memory Learning From?
hook: If a recurrent state is really an online learner, then what it trains on matters. This paper argues most fast-weight rules quietly use the wrong (key, value) pair.
key_points: Fast-weight memories and selective state-space models both compress growing context into a fixed state, making the state transition an online learning rule.
Under read-after-write autoregressive semantics, the correct local training example at step t is the prefix-aligned pair (phi(k_{t-1}), v_t).
The common same-step association (phi(k_t), v_t) is still causal — but it optimizes a different internal objective.
The authors derive normalized first-order updates for two objectives: squared-error regression and negative inner product.
That yields the Falcon family: a scalar NLMS update, a per-column extension, and a sliding-window mini-batch variant, each with an inner-product twin.
Reported outcome: competitive language modeling, improved length extrapolation on variable-digit addition.
content_html: Linear attention, fast-weight memories, and selective state-space models all do the same trick: squeeze an ever-growing context into a fixed-size state. Look closely and each state update is a step of online learning — the state is a little model, and every token hands it a training example. Yifan Zhang, Mengdi Wang, Quanquan Gu, Andrew Chi-Chih Yao and colleagues (arXiv, August 2026) ask a question that follows immediately from that view and is usually skipped: which example, exactly?
extra_html: Their answer is that under read-after-write autoregressive semantics — the state is read before it absorbs the current write — the local example revealed at step t is the prefix-aligned pair (phi(k_{t-1}), v_t), not the same-step (phi(k_t), v_t) that most formulations use. The same-step version isn't acausal; it just optimizes a different internal objective than the prefix-prediction one the model is actually trained for. From there the authors derive normalized first-order updates for a squared-error regression objective and a negative inner-product objective, producing the Falcon family: a scalar NLMS update, a per-column extension, and a sliding-window mini-batch update, each with an inner-product twin. Every variant is given in recurrent, masked-parallel, and chunk-parallel form with a numerically stable positive-decay renormalization, so they stay trainable at scale. Empirically the authors report the variants stay competitive at language modeling and improve length extrapolation on variable-digit addition. The paper's more durable contribution is the framing: it separates temporal alignment, plasticity, forgetting, and bounded rehearsal into four knobs you can reason about independently.

related.title: E²-TTT: Expressivity and Efficiency in Test-Time Training
related.hook: Test-time training updates weights while it reads, but chunking for speed throws away the update's temporal structure. A closed-form state transition gets both.

related.title: Feature Learning in Gated Delta Networks at Scale
related.hook: muP lets you tune hyperparameters on a small model and transfer them to a huge one. This paper derives the equivalent rules for gated delta networks, so sub-quadratic models scale without re-tuning.

related.title: Subquadratic Architectures: xLSTM vs. Mamba-2 vs. Gated DeltaNet
related.hook: Transformers pay a quadratic tax on sequence length. Pitting xLSTM, Mamba-2, and Gated DeltaNet head-to-head on hard tasks, xLSTM comes out ahead — and the paper explains why.

prereqs.title: What Are State-Space Models?
prereqs.hook: A compact hidden state summarizes everything seen so far - update it with each new input and you get sequence modeling that scales linearly, not quadratically.

flashcards.prompt: What does it mean to read a recurrent state transition as an online learning rule?
flashcards.back_html: Fast-weight memories and selective state-space models compress an expanding context into a fixed-size state, so each state update is effectively one step of online learning on a local example.

flashcards.prompt: Under read-after-write autoregressive semantics, which local example does the paper say the fast memory should be trained on at step t?

choices.text: The value pair (v_{t-1}, v_t), with keys unused

flashcards.explanation_html: Read-after-write means the state is read before it absorbs step t's write, so the prefix-aligned pair is the right target. The same-step association is still causal, but it optimizes a different internal objective.

flashcards.prompt: What are the two objectives the Falcon update rules are derived from?
flashcards.back_html: Squared-error regression (giving Falcon-1, a scalar NLMS update; Falcon-2, its per-column extension; Falcon-3, a sliding-window mini-batch update) and a negative inner-product objective (the matching 1A/2A/3A variants).

flashcards.prompt: Where do the authors report the clearest empirical gain from the realigned update?

choices.text: Length extrapolation on variable-digit addition, with language modeling merely competitive
A large drop in language-modeling perplexity across all scales
Faster wall-clock inference than softmax attention at short context
Higher accuracy on image classification benchmarks

flashcards.explanation_html: The paper describes representative variants as remaining competitive at language modeling while improving length extrapolation on variable-digit addition — the framing is analytical, not a benchmark sweep.
